name: Waterford
title: Ship Thickness Measurement at Waterford's Belview Port
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at the Port of Waterford, Belview: container feeders, bulk carriers and general cargo ships on the Suir, holds, tanks, piping.
h1: Thickness Gauging for Ships at the Port of Waterford on the River Suir
intro: The Port of Waterford's main terminal is at Belview, on the River Suir downstream of the city, reached through the long estuary that opens to the sea between Hook Head and Dunmore East. Container feeders link it with continental hubs, and bulk carriers and general cargo ships bring grain, feed, fertiliser and other cargoes for the south-east. A river berth sheltered from the open sea suits careful hold and tank work. For each job, technicians travel from India to Belview and gauge the ship alongside.

highlights.h: Feeder rotations on a fixed cycle
highlights.p: Lo-lo container feeders return to Belview on regular rotations from continental hubs, with the next call date known in advance. Upper deck, hatch coamings and scrubber piping can be gauged across several calls, planned weeks ahead from the line's schedule.

Grain, feed and fertiliser carriers discharging at Belview lie in a sheltered tidal river, where work on deck and in tanks is seldom stopped by weather. A discharge lasting more than a day gives time to gauge holds behind the grabs and open ballast tanks in sequence.

Waterford Harbour is the shared estuary of the Suir, the Barrow and the Nore. Ships for Belview follow the Suir branch, while the smaller port of New Ross lies up the Barrow, so a team working in the south-east can reach either on the same trip.

port.h: Port of Waterford: Belview terminal on the tidal Suir
p: Waterford Harbour is a long, sheltered estuary on Ireland's south coast, entered between the Hook Head lighthouse on the Wexford side and the fishing harbour of Dunmore East on the Waterford side. Ships follow a buoyed channel up the estuary past Passage East, where a small car ferry crosses to Ballyhack, to Cheekpoint, where the Barrow joins the Suir. The Port of Waterford's Belview terminal lies a short way up the Suir from that confluence, on the north bank and downstream of the city. The river is tidal along this whole stretch, ships take a pilot, and the passage up the estuary is planned around the tide, especially for deeper-laden ships. Above Belview, the old city quays see little cargo traffic today; the port's working berths, cranes and storage are concentrated at the downstream terminal.

Belview handles lo-lo container traffic, dry bulk and break-bulk for a hinterland that covers much of the south-east and reaches into the Midlands. Container feeders sail regular rotations to the main continental hubs, carrying Irish exports out and imports in for businesses across the region. Dry bulk is dominated by the farming economy: grain, animal feed ingredients and fertiliser arrive by bulk carrier and are stored or bagged in the port area. Break-bulk, timber and project cargo make up much of the rest. The ships range from short-sea coasters to handysize bulk carriers and container feeders, many of them repeat callers seen throughout the year. Further up the Barrow, the separate port of New Ross takes smaller cargo ships, and Dunmore East at the harbour mouth is a working fishing harbour.

For inspection, Belview's strengths are shelter and regularity. Container feeders call to a published schedule, so a programme can be split across calls with the next visit known in advance. Bulk carriers discharge over one or more days at a river berth where the ship lies steady, which suits hold and tank work carried out behind the cargo operation. Winter gales from the south and south-west can keep ships outside the estuary or delay their passage upriver, but once a ship is alongside the work is rarely interrupted by weather. There is no drydock at Waterford, so dockings for ships in this trade take place at yards in Britain or on the Continent, and Belview gauging is usually the advance work that tells the owner and the yard what to expect when the ship arrives.

facilities.h: Where gauging is done at Belview and in the estuary
p: At the container terminal, feeders are worked by the terminal's cranes, and gauging is planned around the stowage: upper deck plating and hatch coamings in bays that have been worked, lashing bridges and container fittings with MPI where cracking is suspected, and engine-room and scrubber piping while the main engine is stopped. At the bulk berths, the team follows the discharge, measuring each hold once it is empty and clean, and enters ballast tanks under the ship's permit system as the crew releases them.

If a ship has to anchor in the lower harbour to wait for the tide or for a berth, it lies in sheltered water, and launch boarding there is more practical than at an open-sea anchorage, although the estuary's tidal streams are strong and the agent chooses the timing. For anything needing dry access, such as the bottom shell, sea chests, rudder or propeller, the ship has to dock elsewhere. In that case we gauge the internal structure at Belview first, so the yard has a steel estimate in hand before the docking begins.
list: Belview container terminal — hatch coaming, upper deck and scrubber piping gauging on lo-lo feeders during cargo work.
Belview bulk berths — hold, hopper and topside tank gauging on grain, feed and fertiliser carriers behind the discharge.
General cargo and break-bulk berths — hatch cover and deck readings on timber and project cargo ships.
Lower harbour anchorage — launch-borne deck and tank readings on ships waiting for the tide, when the stream allows.
Repeated feeder calls — staged programmes that build a complete pre-docking dataset over several rotations.

context.h: Regulation and trading conditions at the Port of Waterford
p: Waterford is an Irish port within the EU, with port state control carried out by the Department of Transport's Marine Survey Office under the Paris MoU. Container feeders and bulk carriers calling at Belview are selected for inspection on the same risk profile used across the Paris MoU region, and older bulk carriers in particular draw attention to hold structure, hatch covers and ballast tanks. The Enhanced Survey Programme applies to those bulk carriers, so their renewal surveys require extensive thickness measurement and close-up survey, and an owner planning one gains a great deal from knowing hold condition well before the ship reaches the yard.

Since the start of 2021, ships under non-EU flags calling at EU ports have had to carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials, and that applies at Belview as at any Irish port. Feeders on rotations between Waterford and continental hubs trade entirely between EU ports, so all of their emissions on those legs fall under the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime, while ships that also call at British ports count those legs at half. Where a feeder runs an exhaust gas cleaning system, corroded wash-water lines are among the defects owners most want to find before they fail, because a leak at the overboard discharge can force an unplanned stop.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs at Waterford
jobs.p: Belview work is a mix of scheduled and single-call jobs. Feeder operators use the regular rotation to stage pre-docking gauging and piping checks without a dedicated stop. Bulk carrier owners and managers commission hold and tank gauging during discharge ahead of intermediate and renewal surveys, or as condition checks before a sale or a charter. For bulk carriers under the ESP, we follow the extent the class has set for the coming survey. Each job is planned with the superintendent and the ship's agent, the TM plan and order of work are agreed, and the report is issued in class TM formats so the readings can go straight to the yard and the attending surveyor.
list: Pre-docking gauging on a container feeder, split across several Belview calls on its regular rotation.
Hold, hopper and topside tank gauging on a handysize bulk carrier discharging grain, ahead of an ESP intermediate survey.
Scrubber wash-water and overboard piping UT on a feeder during a call, so spools can be ordered before the docking.
Owner's condition gauging on a fertiliser carrier before a decision on steel renewal or sale.
Hatch cover and coaming readings on a general cargo ship after water ingress was reported on the voyage.

logistics: Dublin Airport and Cork Airport are the usual arrival points for a Waterford job, with the onward journey by road or rail; Waterford city has a railway station on the line from Dublin. Ireland issues its own visas, separate from the Schengen area and the UK, so the team travels from India on Irish visas once the dates are confirmed. Access to the Belview terminal and, where needed, a launch for the lower harbour are arranged through the ship's agent.

faqs.q: Can container feeders be gauged at Belview without delaying them?
faqs.a: Yes, by staging the work across calls. Feeder rotations bring the same ship back to Belview at known intervals, so on each call we take a defined part of the scope, such as coamings in worked bays, a ballast tank prepared on passage, or engine-room piping. The readings are referenced to the same frames every time and combined into one report before the docking.

faqs.q: Is the river berth at Belview affected by weather?
faqs.a: Much less than an open-sea berth. Once a ship is alongside in the Suir, work on deck and in tanks continues in most conditions. Weather matters more for arrival, because southerly gales can hold ships outside the estuary and the tide governs the passage upriver. We confirm the expected berthing time with the agent before the team travels.

faqs.q: Where do ships trading to Waterford go for drydocking?
faqs.a: There is no drydock at Waterford, and ships trading to the port dock at yards in Britain or on the Continent. Gauging at Belview in the weeks before a docking gives the yard a steel estimate and lets the superintendent decide which work needs the dock and which can be done afloat, which shortens the docking itself.

faqs.q: Can you also cover New Ross or Dunmore East on the same trip?
faqs.a: Often, yes. New Ross on the River Barrow takes smaller cargo ships, and Dunmore East at the harbour entrance is a fishing harbour, both within reach of Belview by road. If a fleet has ships at more than one of these ports in the same week, we plan the visit so that one team covers them, with access arranged through each ship's agent.
